To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we performed the first study to evaluate copy number variants as modifiers of cancer risk for women carrying pathogenic BRCA1 mutations.

we have identified four genomic loci that are associated with increased risk of breast cancer in BRCA pathogenic variant carriers (GTF2, ZNF, NAALAD2 and PSG5) and two loci that are protective of ovarian cancer in BRACA pathogenic variant carriers.

we identified a number of genomic deletions that are likely to influence risk of breast or/and ovarian cancer in BRC1 pathogenic variant mutation carriers, and that the most interesting finding was a deletion in the CYP2 family, which has a plausible biological mechanism in ovarian cancer risk.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying genetic variants associated with breast cancer risk in BRCA1 mutation carriers.
the identification of genomic loci that modify breast and ovarian cancer risks for BRCA1 mutation carriers.
the identification of genetic variants that modify cancer risk among BRCA1 pathogenetic variant carriers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this study provides evidence for the existence of copy-number variants that modify risk of cancer in BRCA pathogenic variant carriers.
the study did not identify any CNVs with strong associations with breast or ovarian cancers in BRCA1 carriers, but that it did identify some loci with potential associations.
the study does provide evidence of CNVs as modifiers of breast cancer risk for BRCAA1 carriers, but the study also highlights the difficulties of CNV detection and validation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CNVs are not a common source of genetic variation in BRCA1 mutation carriers and do not appear to play a major role in modifying cancer risk.
CNV analysis of BRCA1 pathogen carriers identified several loci associated with breast or ovarian risk.
we identified several CNV deletions that are associated with breast or ovarian cancers in BRCA1 carriers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CNV studies are challenging, but they can be informative in the context of cancer risk prediction for individuals carrying pathogenic variants.
the CNVs we identified may be used to develop risk stratification models to identify BRCA1 carriers at increased or decreased risk of cancer.

the use of CNV calling algorithms to detect CNV deletions in large cohorts of patients carrying pathogen variant in BRCA1 and BRCA2 is a viable approach for identifying novel genetic modifiers of risk.
